results.note: ¶43 verbatim: 'you are not an employee—you are in a business with one employee: yourself'; ¶46 'nobody owes you a career. You own it as a sole proprietor'; ¶48 (within ±2) applies the output discipline to the career questions.

¶4 best-run company in technology, ¶5 self-made rise, ¶6 wrote it personally (no ghostwriter), ¶11 the three aspects of genius: one-sentence compression, brand-new ideas, teaches greatness not mere competency.

¶20 'all of them possess a basically similar flow of activity'; ¶10 build backward from the longest step and offset the others; ¶34 detect and fix at the lowest-value stage; ¶35 (within ±2) the criminal-justice example.

The example is exact (¶43: Intel division stagger chart of month-by-month re-forecast incoming orders), but the 'leading indicators... in time for corrective action' framing comes from ¶38-40, outside ¶43±2; the window itself supports anticipating trends, not the corrective-action clause.

ch05 ¶81-84 the L1×A1+L2×A2 equation and shifting the activity mix toward high leverage; ch18 ¶9 training as highest-leverage activity; ch15 ¶11 appraisal as one of the manager's highest-leverage activities — the instruments are all cast in the same leverage calculus.

¶4 near-verbatim: both basic managerial tasks 'can only occur during face-to-face encounters, and therefore only during meetings'; meeting is 'the medium through which managerial work is performed'; use the time as efficiently as possible.

ch07 ¶4-6 knowledge/position power divergence in know-how businesses; ¶8-11 free discussion, clear decision, full support; ¶13 lowest competent level (within ±2); ¶29-30 decision as output and the six questions verbatim.
¶41-42 exact: Columbus's key results 'came in like clockwork' but he missed his objective, yet performed well — the MBO system 'is not a legal document upon which to base a performance review.'
¶7 exact: regional egg purchasing centers as the compromise; ¶6-9 settle advertising, hiring, machinery, menu, real estate each on its own terms — no blanket rule.

¶19 Grove's Law verbatim; ¶8 the responsiveness-vs-leverage balancing act (Sloan quote); ¶25-27 allocation of shared resources, central allocators rejected via Hungary, middle managers named as the answer.

¶10 operating priorities from the general manager plus a technical supervisory relationship — 'The solution is dual reporting'; ¶11 (within ±2) the peer group as supervisor; ¶15-16 ambiguity disliked, 'people will strive to find something simpler... it doesn't exist.'
¶12 exact: an engineer's worth in a group 'cannot be pinned down by appealing to the free market'; buying engineering work 'by the bit' would cost more than the contribution is worth.
¶32-33 exact: the ring-toss experiment, researchers classifying gamblers, conservatives, and achievers who 'had to test the limits of what they could do.'

¶6 TRM as the fundamental variable; ¶9 the three styles by TRM level plus monitoring; ¶10 (within ±2) 'do not make a value judgment' about structured style; ¶26 raise TRM rapidly — high-TRM style takes less time and increases managerial leverage.

ch15 ¶11-12 review as the single most important task-relevant feedback, highest leverage, purpose = improving the subordinate's performance; ch17 ¶6 bonus percentage scaled to level, ¶13-15 merit-diverging curves and promotion on performance; ch16 ¶7 interviewing 'just about impossible' vs appraisal, ¶30-31 the quit conversation.

¶27 exact: Grove's most careful, thorough interview produced a hire who 'from day one... was a disaster'; careful interviewing 'doesn't guarantee you anything, it merely increases your odds of getting lucky.'
¶14 exact: Americans accept that someone must finish last in a race, but at work competitive ranking 'becomes a highly charged issue' — cultural, not logical.

¶5 inefficiencies, excess costs, unhappy customers, dangerous situations from undertrained employees; ¶7-9 training + motivation as the only two levers, training among the highest-leverage activities; ¶12-14 process not event, tied to actual practice, believable practicing authority and role model — the manager.
¶3 exact: 'if you do at least 100 points worth of what you find here, you'll be a distinctly better manager for it'; ¶2 reading is the down payment, the assignments must be performed honestly.

¶31-32 exact: Intel's four 25% quarters (production, support, administration, design/sales) and the finding that 'all our employees produce in some sense,' with production discipline applied to all of it.
